title: Decision-making under uncertainty
summary: Applying computer science to human decisions: when to stop searching, how to balance exploring against exploiting, sorting and caching, scheduling, Bayesian prediction, overfitting, constraint relaxation, deliberate randomness, and strategic interaction.
scope: deciding when to stop searching and commit
predicting from sparse evidence and choosing priors
overfitting, and when to deliberately think less
simplifying an intractable problem by relaxing constraints
using randomness deliberately in search and decision-making
designing protocols, queues and backoff under congestion
anticipating other people's strategies and reducing their cognitive load

packs.title: Algorithms to Live By
packs.author: Brian Christian & Tom Griffiths
caveats: Popular-science synthesis, not a primary source. It reports results from optimal stopping, bandit theory, scheduling and Bayesian statistics accurately but informally; cite it for the decision heuristic, not for a proof.
Numeric thresholds (37%, Gittins indices, Bayes rules) assume the stated model. Check the assumptions hold before transferring a constant.

chapters.title: Introduction: Algorithms to Live By
chapters.source: Christian & Griffiths, *Algorithms to Live By* (HarperCollins, 2016), Introduction.
chapters.governs: the frame for every other chapter — what an algorithm is, when borrowing one from computer science is legitimate, and what the book actually claims.
chapters.thesis: the hardest problems in human life have the **same computational structure** as the hardest problems in computer science, because both are what happens when a finite agent acts in finite space and time. Where the structures match, the algorithms transfer.

chapters.governs: when to stop searching and commit, in any process where options arrive one at a time and passing means losing them.
chapters.thesis: the hard part of a search is not *which* option to pick — it is *how many* to consider before picking. That question has a closed-form answer, and the answer depends almost entirely on what information you have and what waiting costs.

chapters.thesis: the explore/exploit balance is not a matter of temperament. It is set almost entirely by **the interval** — how long you will be around to enjoy what you learn. Change the interval and the correct behaviour inverts.

chapters.title: Sorting
chapters.source: Christian & Griffiths, *Algorithms to Live By* (HarperCollins, 2016), Ch. 3.
chapters.governs: whether to impose order at all, and if so at what cost — over information, possessions, and people.
chapters.thesis: sorting has **dis**economies of scale, and its only justification is the searching it saves later. Since search is often cheap, **the right amount of order is frequently less than none at all**. And when what is being sorted is people, the choice between comparison and measurement is the choice between a fight and a race.

chapters.governs: what to keep close to hand, what to evict, and where to put things — across storage, workspaces, supply chains and memory.
chapters.thesis: forgetting is not failure; it is **cache management**, and it has a provably good policy. The nearest thing available to clairvoyance is to assume **history repeats itself backwards** — what you used most recently is what you will need next.

chapters.title: Bayes's Rule
chapters.source: Christian & Griffiths, *Algorithms to Live By* (HarperCollins, 2016), Ch. 6.
chapters.governs: predicting from very little evidence — often a single observation — and knowing which prediction rule the situation calls for.
chapters.thesis: **the shape of the prior decides the prediction rule.** Three distributions give three completely different, mutually contradictory rules of thumb, and picking the wrong one is the main way single-observation forecasts go wrong. Our days are full of *small* data, and we handle it well only because our priors are quietly rich.

chapters.title: Overfitting
chapters.source: Christian & Griffiths, *Algorithms to Live By* (HarperCollins, 2016), Ch. 7.
chapters.governs: how hard to think, how many factors to weigh, and how much to trust any measurement standing in for what you actually care about.
chapters.thesis: **a better fit to the data you have is not a better prediction.** Wherever the thing you can measure differs from the thing you care about — which is nearly always — optimising harder makes results worse, not merely less efficient. chapters.source: Christian & Griffiths, *Algorithms to Live By* (HarperCollins, 2016), Ch. 8.
chapters.governs: what to do once a problem is proven too hard to solve exactly — which is the normal case for real optimisation.
chapters.thesis: when the perfect answer is unreachable, **neither grind forever nor give up: solve a deliberately easier problem instead.** Relaxation is wishful thinking done *consciously*, with the bonus that it yields bounds telling you how far from optimal you actually are.

chapters.title: Computational Kindness
chapters.source: Christian & Griffiths, *Algorithms to Live By* (HarperCollins, 2016), Conclusion.
chapters.governs: how to judge your own decisions after the fact, and how to design problems — for yourself and for other people — that are cheap to solve.
chapters.thesis: three things follow from taking the computational view seriously. Some algorithms transfer directly. **A good process is a defence even when the outcome is bad.** And since we hand each other computational problems constantly, we can choose to hand over easy ones — *"computation is bad,"* and reducing someone's mental labour is a form of kindness.

rules.text: **Ask first whether the problem has a known structure.** Many everyday dilemmas are recognised, named, and solved classes — not novel personal predicaments.
**Distinguish problems where information can be gathered freely from those where gathering it costs the option.** The second class has entirely different optimal strategies.
**Treat "find the right balance" as an unfinished answer.** The useful version specifies where the balance is.
**Do not equate rigour with exhaustiveness.** For hard problems the best available methods use approximation, randomness and early stopping *by design*.
**Trade accuracy against time deliberately** rather than treating any shortfall from optimal as failure.
**Read a mistake as evidence about the problem before reading it as evidence about yourself.** Difficulty is a property of problems, and many are provably hard.
**Expect the hard cases.** Uncertainty, deadlines, partial information and a changing world are the normal human condition, not the exception.

**Borrow the vocabulary even when you cannot borrow the numbers.** Naming the structure — stopping, explore/exploit, caching, scheduling — is most of the benefit when the situation is too messy to quantify.
**Judge process, not only outcome.** A provably optimal method still fails often; that is not evidence against the method.
**Ask "how many options should I consider?" before "which option should I pick?"** The second question is downstream of the first, and only the first has a closed-form answer.
**Name both failure modes — stopping early and stopping late — before choosing a policy.** A rule that only guards against one is not a solution.
**With ordinal information only, use Look-Then-Leap at ~37%.** Anything between 35% and 40% performs nearly identically, so do not over-tune the constant.
**Expect to fail ~63% of the time and do not treat that as evidence the method is broken.** Optimal play still misses the best option most of the time.

**Prefer any objective yardstick to a subjective one.** Converting a no-information game into a full-information one raises the success rate from 37% to 58% — a far larger gain than better judgement inside the no-information game.

**With full information, drop the look phase entirely and use a declining threshold.** Standards should fall as options run out, and by a computable amount — never below average until you are genuinely out of options.
**When maximising value rather than finding the best, set the threshold from the cost of waiting alone**, and note it depends on the *spread* of outcomes, not their level.
**A value-maximising threshold never declines with bad luck.** If the odds and the search cost are unchanged, a run of poor offers is not information.
**Never reconsider an option you passed on.** What you spent searching is sunk; if it was below threshold then, it is below threshold now.
**If offers can be rejected, start offering much earlier** (25% rather than 37%) and keep offering to every best-yet candidate.
**If passed options can be recalled, look longer** (61%) and keep an explicit fallback to the best one that got away.
**Stop pressing a repeatable gamble at roughly (success odds ÷ failure odds) attempts.**
**Do not target full utilisation of a contended resource.** The last 5% of occupancy can double everyone's search time; slack is what makes the system usable.
**When the optimal policy under a model implies certain ruin, reject the model.** Some problems are better avoided than solved.
**Before calling behaviour suboptimal, check for an unmodelled cost of time.** A 1% per-observation search cost fully explains apparently premature stopping.
**Establish the interval before choosing a strategy.** Nothing else in this problem matters as much, and it is the input people most often leave implicit.
**Explore early, exploit late** — the value of exploring only falls and the value of exploiting only rises.
**Never treat a recurring decision as isolated.** Maximising the expected value of this choice alone is correct only if it is genuinely your last.
**Read someone's explore/exploit ratio as a statement about their perceived interval**, including your own and your organisation's. A sudden shift to sure things is a horizon signal.
**Keep win-stay, drop lose-shift.** A single failure is weak evidence against an option with a long record.
**Give untested options a bonus over their expected value.** An unknown is worth more than a known equal, because the upside is still live.
**Prefer Upper Confidence Bound in practice**: choose by the best an option could plausibly be, not the best it has been. It needs no discounting assumption and is computable in your head.
**Optimism, bounded by evidence, is the rational default** and the best available protection against regret.
**Minimise regret rather than maximise payoff** when the horizon is long — and note that regret accrues most heavily from *not trying*.
**Expect regret to keep growing even under optimal play**; judge a strategy by the growth *rate*, which should be logarithmic and decelerating.

**Do not default to fixed-allocation experiments.** An even split knowingly keeps half your subjects on the worse option for the whole test; adapt allocation as evidence accrues unless a decisive answer is worth that cost.
**Watch for over-exploration in recurring choices** — the empirical bias runs opposite to the stopping bias, and people observe far longer than the math warrants.
**When the environment is non-stationary, never stop exploring entirely**; periodically revisit options you wrote off, because the world may have changed.
**Do not read exploratory behaviour as incompetence.** Judge behaviour against the phase of the interval it belongs to.
**Take advice about *what is good* from long explorers; do not copy their current *behaviour*.** Their conclusions transfer; their exploit-phase habits do not.
**Expect dis-economies of scale in any ordering task.** Doubling the batch more than doubles the work, which inverts the usual instinct to batch things up.
**Reduce the batch before optimising the method.** Sorting more often in smaller quantities beats a cleverer algorithm most of the time.
**Analyse the worst case, not the average or the best,** whenever you need to make a guarantee.
**Judge cost by growth class, not by constants** — but remember Big-O deliberately ignores constants, so it misleads at small n.
**Never sort what you will not search.** Sorting the unsearched is total waste; searching the unsorted is merely inefficient. Given uncertainty, **err toward messiness**.

**Justify heavy up-front sorting against three conditions**: it will certainly be searched, repeatedly, and sort time is cheaper than search time. Google clears all three; your bookshelf and inbox clear none.
**As search gets cheaper, sorting loses value.** Reassess filing habits whenever search improves, rather than carrying them forward.
**Use coarse buckets before fine ordering**, and derive the buckets from the known distribution — good buckets split the load evenly, bad ones achieve nothing.
**Do not confuse a single-elimination winner with a ranking.** Such a format determines first place and leaves everything else unsorted; second place is not evidence.
**Under noisy comparison, prefer robust methods over efficient ones.** Efficiency moves items far per comparison, so early errors become permanent.
**Trust accumulated round-robin standings over knockout results.** The long tally is the fault-tolerant measurement; the bracket is a lottery weighted by skill.
**Compute how much a series result actually establishes** before treating it as evidence of quality — six 70% rounds confer only ~12% confidence.
**Minimising comparisons is not always the objective.** Where the comparisons themselves have value, or where sustained uncertainty is the product, more of them is correct.
**Expect conflict to grow super-linearly with group size**, and treat capping group size as a legitimate intervention.
**Do not remove a group's means of resolving rank** and expect less conflict; an unfinishable sort produces more.

**Replace comparison with measurement wherever possible.** Any shared benchmark — however crude — converts a fight into a race and collapses the cost of establishing status from linearithmic to constant.
**Build a hierarchy rather than choosing between fast and large.** Small-and-fast backed by large-and-slow beats either alone, and applies to physical storage as much as digital.
**Have a cache even if you cannot manage it well.** Random eviction is far better than nothing; do not let policy debates block the basic structure.
**Evict by Least Recently Used, not First In First Out.** "When did I last use it?" is a much better question than "how long have I had it?", though both sound equally sensible.
**Assume temporal locality unless you know otherwise** — what was just used is most likely to be used next, and the longest-untouched is the safest to discard.
**Treat recency as your substitute for clairvoyance.** Where the future is unknown, the reversed past is the best available predictor.
**Cache by proximity, not just by speed.** When nearness is the scarce resource, keeping copies near the point of use is the whole win.
**Place items in the cache closest to where they are used**, even when that violates category logic. Vacuum bags behind the couch beats vacuum bags with the cleaning supplies.
**Add levels above and below your main cache**, and demote between them by LRU.
**Do not group like with like by default.** Content-based grouping costs sorting time and delivers no retrieval guarantee.
**Always return a used item to the front.** This bounds your worst-case search time at twice the theoretical optimum — a guarantee no other placement rule provides.
**Recognise a working pile as a self-organising structure**, not disorder to be corrected. Reorganising it by category makes retrieval worse.
**Display collections by last-accessed rather than alphabetically**, wherever the interface allows it.
**Surface what was recently *used*, not what was recently *added*.** Most displays privilege new arrivals; recency of use is the better predictor of demand.
**Predict aggregate demand rather than individual demand** when pre-positioning resources — the law of large numbers makes the group tractable where the person is not.

**Expect retrieval to slow as expertise grows, and do not read it as decline.** A larger store is a harder search problem; the lag is evidence of the size of the archive, not the failure of the mechanism.
**Choose the metric before choosing the schedule.** Without one, no ordering is better than another, and conflicting productivity advice cannot be adjudicated.
**To minimise the worst delay, work by earliest due date** — and note that task durations are irrelevant to this rule, so you need not estimate them.
**To minimise how many things are late, drop the largest scheduled item the moment you fall behind**, and stop worrying about the order of anything already late.
**To shrink a backlog fastest, do the shortest task first.**
**To act on what matters, order by importance divided by duration** — only prioritise something twice as long if it is twice as important.
**Decide whether you are minimising the amount or the count** before choosing a strategy — it is the difference between the debt avalanche and the debt snowball, and neither is universally right.
**Read procrastination as a metric error, not a character flaw.** Clearing trivia is optimal behaviour for minimising task *count*; fix the objective rather than the discipline.
**Audit the metrics your tools impose on you.** Unread badges silently weight everything equally; if you cannot change what they count, remove them.
**Watch for priority inversion** — if the important thing is stalled, find what is blocking it, and promote the blocker to the priority of the thing it blocks.
**Treat a blocking trivial task as the most important task.** "Never let what matters most be at the mercy of what matters least" is false under precedence constraints.
**Schedule back to front when tasks have prerequisites**, placing last the unblocked task with the latest due date.
**Expect most real scheduling problems to be intractable** — 84% of classified ones are — and use these rules as good starting points rather than expecting optimality.
**Prefer reacting to planning when the future is uncertain.** Foreknowledge can make the optimal schedule uncomputable while on-the-fly rules stay easy and nearly as good.
**Count context switches as pure loss.** Interrupting someone more than a few times an hour can reduce their output to nothing.
**Protect blocks long enough to reload context** — for demanding work, anything under about ninety minutes is largely spent on reloading.
**Recognise thrashing by its signature**: full effort, no progress, and no spare capacity to reorganise. Performance collapses rather than degrading.
**When thrashing, lower the quality of your prioritisation, not your effort.** Choosing what to do next can cost more than doing it; arbitrary order beats paralysis.
**Refuse work whose working set will not fit**, before the collapse rather than after.
**Set a minimum time slice** and honour it, so that responsiveness cannot consume throughput entirely.
**Be exactly as responsive as required and no more**, then batch everything else — coalesce bills, mail and messages into scheduled passes rather than servicing each interrupt on arrival.

**Identify the distribution before choosing a prediction rule.** Multiplicative, Average and Additive give contradictory answers; nearly all single-observation errors are shape errors, not arithmetic errors.
**Use the Multiplicative Rule for scale-free quantities** — grosses, wealth, city sizes, durations of unfamiliar things. The longer it has run, the longer to expect.
**Use the Average Rule for quantities with a natural scale** — predict the mean, and a little beyond once the mean is passed.
**Use the Additive Rule for memoryless processes** — predict a constant increment, and stop looking for the right moment to quit, because there isn't one.
**Apply Laplace's Law, (w+1)/(n+2), for a rate from few trials.** One success from one attempt is 2/3, not certainty.
**Never quote a median without the shape of its tail.** A right-skewed distribution turns "half die within eight months" into a very different personal forecast.
**Use "it will last as long as it has lasted" only when you genuinely know nothing** — including not knowing the timescale. Where you have real knowledge, this rule is actively misleading.
**Calibrate surprise to the distribution.** Under a power law, be *most* alarmed when a long-running thing has run longest; venerability is not safety.
**State your prior explicitly, even as a guess.** Bayes cannot run without one, and refusing to name it does not remove it.
**Reverse-engineer priors from predictions.** What someone expects reveals the distribution their experience taught them, and is measurable where direct data is not.
**Distrust your predictions in domains where you lack exposure.** Failure is not an inference error but an absent prior.
**Read apparent impatience as a possible forecast, not a character defect.** Giving up early is rational when waits are scale-free or the source is unreliable.
**Treat reliability as an input to other people's patience.** Consistently keeping promises changes what others can rationally afford to wait for.
**Guard the inputs that form your priors.** Media frequency is not world frequency; a diet of the unusual will systematically miscalibrate you.
**Judge a model by how it generalises, never by how well it fits what you already have.** Perfect fit is a warning sign, not a result.
**Test stability under perturbation.** Re-fit with slight noise or a different sample; a model that swings wildly is overfitted regardless of its fit statistics.
**Add a factor only if it is significantly better, not merely better.** Complexity must earn its place against an explicit penalty.
**Name the gap between your metric and your goal before optimising.** Every measurement is a proxy; the size of that gap determines how hard you should push.
**Assume that anything you measure and reward will be optimised — including in ways you did not intend.** Perverse outcomes are usually competent optimisation of a badly chosen target.
**Cross-validate on held-out data**, and additionally **cross-validate the metric itself** against a different, harder-to-game evaluation applied to a small sample.
**Treat divergence between your primary metric and your spot-check as the alarm**: rising scores with falling independent assessment means the target has been gamed.
**Drive weak factors to zero rather than shrinking them.** A short list of things that matter beats a long list of things that might.
**Prefer a rule that ignores the data when your estimates are unreliable.** A strategy that never fits the data cannot overfit it — which is why 50/50 can beat optimisation.
**Run the regularize check explicitly**: are the quantities I am relying on hard to estimate, and does my method put heavy weight on them? If yes, simplify.
**Treat time spent deliberating as a complexity knob.** More time means more factors and more overfitting, not automatically a better decision.
**Bound deliberation in advance** — to a page, a timebox, a fixed number of factors — and decide when the bound is reached.
**Trust the first factors you generate.** If the earliest considerations are the most important, later ones mostly add noise.
**Match your tool's resolution to your certainty.** Use a blunt instrument early; fine detail invites precision you have not earned.
**Value historical constraint as robustness, not as inefficiency.** Being imperfectly adapted to the present is what survives changes in the present.
**Discount fast-moving consensus.** Rapid information flow enables rapid overfitting at the scale of a whole culture.
**Establish whether the problem is tractable before committing effort to an exact answer.** Difficulty is a measurable property, and many ordinary problems have no efficient solution.
**Treat intractability as a change of method, not as defeat.** The response is to relax, not to abandon or to grind.
**Solve the problem you wish you had first**, then bring the constraints back. If you cannot solve what is in front of you, solve an easier version and see whether it offers a starting point.
**Use the relaxed answer as a bound.** Knowing the best conceivable outcome tells you how far from optimal your practical answer is, without ever finding the optimum.
**Ask the fantasy questions deliberately** — what would you do without the fear, the money constraint, the travel time — as an analytical step rather than as consolation.
**When forced into either/or, imagine the blend, then round.** A fractional solution is not an answer, but converting it back is usually cheap and often provably close.
**Convert probabilities into decisions where averages cannot apply**, rather than discarding a fractional result as meaningless.
**Accept a bounded multiple of optimal.** Twice the optimal number of invitations or vaccinations, computed quickly, beats an unattainable perfect answer.
**Ask "or else what?" of every hard constraint.** Turning a prohibition into a priced penalty is what makes an intractable problem tractable.
**Audit which constraints are genuinely inviolable.** Stated absolutes frequently turn out to have been violated repeatedly and forgotten — check the record before designing around them.
**Consider paying a known penalty rather than accepting a large loss** to satisfy a rule; and note that merely imagining the infraction clarifies the real cost.
**Expect a good process to surface options nobody proposed.** The value of optimisation on an intractable problem is often the unconsidered arrangement, not the optimum.

**Distinguish conscious from unconscious wishful thinking.** Relaxation works because it is designed to be reconciled with reality; fantasy that is never reconciled ends in the collapse Booker describes.
**Sample when the possibility space is too large to enumerate.** An estimate with known error beats an exact answer you will never compute.
**Judge sampling by whether it returns an answer at all**, not by whether it beats exhaustive analysis for precision.
**Simulate the process rather than deriving it** when outcomes branch — play the game, run the trial, count what happens.
**Use repeated random tests to drive uncertainty arbitrarily low.** Each independent check multiplies down the error; near-certainty is usually cheap.
**Decide explicitly what error rate you need** rather than assuming you need none — cryptography settles for one in 10²⁴, and that is a choice.
**Trade certainty for time and space deliberately.** Error probability is a third design axis, not a defect.

**Prefer random samples to both anecdotes and aggregates.** Selected stories carry no information *because* they were selected; aggregates hide the heterogeneity that matters, and you rarely know which statistic to ask for.
**Commit in advance to publishing what the random sample returns**, whatever it says — the pre-commitment is what makes it evidence.
**Treat a large quantitative gap as a qualitative one.** "Possible in principle" is not a defence when the cost is astronomically large.
**Recognise the local maximum**: nothing nearby improves matters, yet you suspect something far better exists. Nearby-optimal is not optimal.
**Accept a temporary worsening to escape.** Some traps require moving *away* from the exit before you can reach it.
**Match the escape to the landscape** — jitter for small perturbations, full random restart where local maxima are dense, Metropolis-style occasional bad moves for continuous search.
**Anneal: be most random early and least random late**, and slow down as you approach a decision rather than after it.
**Never decline a clear improvement**, however random your process otherwise is.
**Scale willingness to try a bad option inversely to how bad it is** — this keeps exploration cheap rather than reckless.
**Engineer serendipity deliberately.** Random inputs — cards, articles, unfamiliar ingredients — break context and are a reliable technique, not a happy accident.
**Prefer many independent paths to one reliable channel.** Redundant routing makes reliability *increase* with scale, where a dedicated channel makes it decrease.
**Accept that confirmation is never complete** and fix a practical stopping point, rather than pursuing certainty that provably cannot exist.
**Treat acknowledgment as load-bearing.** Backchannel traffic is not overhead; a sender starved of it slows down or stops.
**Tune silence-to-alarm thresholds to the medium's round-trip time**, and state them where the other party cannot infer them.
**Do not eliminate the signals that prove a channel is alive.** Removing background reassurance forces both parties into constant explicit checking.
**Break symmetry with randomness** when two parties keep colliding through polite deference.
**Retry with exponentially increasing delays** rather than a fixed number of attempts. Retry rate approaches zero while never becoming refusal.
**Replace "three strikes and you're out" with backoff** wherever you want finite patience and infinite mercy — it protects you from an endless cycle without declaring anyone beyond redemption.
**Prefer immediate small escalating sanctions to delayed large ones.** Predictable and prompt beats severe and rare — HOPE cut new arrests by half and drug use by 72%.
**Increase commitment additively, cut it multiplicatively.** Ramp gently, retreat by half — asymmetry is what makes a shared system stable.
**Pull back at least as fast as you are being overloaded**, or the system cannot stabilise.
**Consider reversible movement in both directions** rather than one-way promotion or termination. Aim for a sawtooth, not an arc.
**Push to the point of failure only when your response to failure is sharp and resilient.** Otherwise do not.
**Judge listening as participation.** A distracted audience measurably degrades what the speaker produces.
**Keep queues small and drain them to empty.** A permanently full buffer delivers all the latency and none of the smoothing.
**Preserve the feedback that overload generates.** Refusing work is how a system learns to slow down; absorbing everything hides the signal until far too late.
**Make refusal explicit rather than deferring indefinitely.** Rejecting now is often kinder and more useful than a reply guaranteed too late to matter.
**Distinguish capacity from responsiveness.** For anything interactive, turnaround time matters more than throughput — and only one of them gets advertised.
**Stop escalating levels of "what do they think I think."** Simulating a system as complex as yourself exhausts your resources by definition.
**Play one level above your opponent, not more.** Over-modelling attributes information to people who do not have it, and makes your own signals unreadable.
**Watch for opponents who profit from your deliberation.** Where thinking is costly and time-bounded, an adversary can win by giving you nothing worth thinking about.
**Compute the equilibrium instead of reading the person** where one is available — but treat "an equilibrium exists" as no guarantee anyone can find it.
**Discount predictions built on equilibria that are intractable to compute.** If it cannot be found, it cannot be relied on as a forecast of behaviour.
**Never assume a stable outcome is a good one.** Stability is what makes bad equilibria resistant, not what makes them desirable.
**Prefer dominant strategies where they exist** — they remove the need to model anyone else at all.
**Estimate the price of anarchy before demanding coordination.** Sometimes central control adds only a third; sometimes its absence is ruinous.
**Recognise the commons structure**: private gain, diffuse harm, and a race that leaves everyone worse off with no relative advantage gained.
**Do not try to fix a bad equilibrium from inside it.** Change the rules, or find an outside authority who can.
**Making outcomes worse can make everyone better off** if it moves the equilibrium. Constraints are not merely costs.
**Sweetening a payoff without moving the equilibrium accomplishes nothing.** Check whether your incentive changes the *structure* or merely the stakes.
**Set floors rather than offering rewards** in races to the bottom — a compulsory minimum costs nothing and works where a bonus fails.
**Bind yourself deliberately.** Contracts, schedules, closing times and commitments are equilibrium-shifting devices, not just restrictions.
**Treat involuntary commitment as an asset.** A reputation for responding disproportionately deters exploitation; predictability of feeling substitutes for external enforcement.
**Beware when public information exceeds private information** — when you know what others are doing but not why, you may be joining a cascade rather than learning.
**Broadcast your doubts even when you act with the crowd**, so your action does not read as confidence and stop being informative.
**Remember that a cascade requires no irrationality or malice.** Assigning blame after a collapse may simply be the wrong frame.

**Design for truthfulness.** If you do not want people optimising against you, optimise for them — any game requiring strategic misrepresentation can in principle be rebuilt so that honesty dominates.
**Count strategising as a cost of the game itself**, and prefer arrangements that let you act on what you actually want.
**Evaluate decisions by the process, not the outcome.** A provably optimal method still fails often; if you followed the best available process, the loss is not a mistake.
**State the failure rate of your method up front.** 37% optimal means 63% failure, and knowing that in advance is what makes a bad outcome bearable rather than evidence against the method.
**Recognise that even perfect information would not guarantee success** in many of these problems — the ceiling is lower than intuition assumes.
**Accept "good enough" on intractable problems** rather than paying unbounded cost for an answer you cannot reach.
**Choose tractable problems where you have the choice.** Complexity awareness is a filter on which situations to enter, not only a method for handling them.
**Treat every request you make as a computational problem you are imposing**, and minimise its cost — this is the core move.
**Prefer verification to search when asking something of someone.** A concrete proposal to accept or decline is far cheaper than an open-ended question.
**Offer constrained options, even somewhat arbitrary ones.** "Tuesday 1–2pm" gets more yeses than "any time that works."
**State your preferences rather than withholding them.** "I'm flexible" passes the cognitive buck and forces others to simulate your mind — the most expensive computation there is.
**Reduce the number of options you present**, and let others eliminate rather than construct.
**Beware of consensus assembled from mutual inference.** Groups reach decisions nobody wanted when each person mirrors the enthusiasm they read in the others.
**Design so the greedy algorithm stays optimal.** A slightly worse arrangement that keeps the decision simple usually beats an optimal one that makes every user solve a hard problem.
**Audit designs for the mental labour they impose**, alongside space, materials and money — the cost is real and rarely counted.
**Replace spinning with blocking wherever the waiting is done by people.** Notify rather than making people watch; convert a continuous re-decision into a single one.
**Publish the information that collapses a repeated inference into one decision** — a countdown, an ETA, a confirmed time.
**Stop treating assumption, approximation and chance as compromises.** On hard problems they are what rationality consists of.
